cells.tense: Right now you're the one holding all of it at once — every feeling on offer — and you're not drowning in it.
cells.ask: Name one pattern in what keeps drawing you — what the same pull keeps turning out to be — out loud, once, before you decide anything.
cells.core:
You can hold a whole spread of feeling in front of you without losing the thread. The options are real, they're not a fog, and you're steady enough in them to let the day end on them — which most people can't do; most people need an answer by tonight. What you've got is the rare version: many feelings present, none of them running you.

That steadiness is free to feed something next. Say one pattern out loud — the thing the same pull keeps turning out to be — before you pick anything. It's not a decision and nobody hears it but you; it just puts a name on what was already organizing the spread from underneath. Once it's named, the next ending comes easier.

cells.verb: gathering every feeling that might be chosen
cells.place: the point where what's been gathered is finished being held and can be let go

cells.tense: You're already living past the point where this gets decided — bracing for how it'll land before it's had a chance to land.
cells.ask: Pick one of the possibilities and leave it on the table for a day — no counting, no comparing, no quietly arranging for it to win — and notice what staying still with it holds.
cells.core:
You've got so many feelings on the table that you've started pre-deciding all of them. What gets thought about is how each one would land, what it would cost, how it would look — and the looking-ahead is doing the deciding now. The possibilities were supposed to stay open a little longer; you're racing them to an ending they haven't reached.

When it's working, this is just gathering — nothing has to be settled yet and the not-settling doesn't frighten you. Try that size: choose one possibility and hold it steady for a day. Not weighing it, not testing it. Just leave it where it is and see what holding it still does, because the endings here can't be rushed into being real.

cells.tense: You're still standing where the last ending was, and the feelings on offer now haven't been let all the way in.
cells.ask: Take one feeling that's been hovering and give it a plain sentence — what it is, in your own words — before you file it away.
cells.core:
There's plenty being offered and it isn't reaching you. Something closed at the last ending and stayed closed, so now the possibilities come and go without landing — nothing pulls, nothing repels, it's all just passing at a distance. The emptiness isn't the feelings being gone. It's that nothing in you is picking them up.

This isn't fixed by feeling harder; that just pushes into a place that's already tired. What's missing is a mind at rest, taking one thing at a time. So take one feeling that's been hovering and say what it is, in plain words, once. Nothing has to follow from saying it. The point is just to get one thing across the distance so the rest of it has somewhere to come to.

cells.tense: You're sorting what's worth feeling as it comes — every day, by instinct — and filing it under how the day happened to go.
cells.ask: Point at one thing you've been drawn to and say, plainly, that you're drawn to it — one sentence, no reason attached.
cells.core:
The gathering runs all the time — which pull to answer, which feeling to let near, which to let pass — and you describe it as something that arrives on its own. It doesn't. You're the one sorting, and the sorting is good: you can tell what's worth reaching for from what's just noise. You do it faster than you can explain it, which is probably why it doesn't get called yours.

Bring it down to the simplest thing. Take one draw you've been treating as automatic — one place, one pull you keep returning to — and say out loud that you're drawn to it. No case for it, no timing, no explaining why it makes sense. It doesn't even have to be a big one. Saying it once puts the name back on work you were already doing.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim I'd flag in my own draft is any sentence that says what the person actually feels about the choices in front of them — the record says possibilities are present and gathering, not that the person is tempted, thrilled, or avoiding; I can describe what's being gathered and what it costs to hold it all open, but not their inner weather. A reader could reasonably object that 'completion that opens rather than closes' sounds like the person is about to finish something big, when this card says nothing about a project at all — so I keep the ending undecided and the act small. The ask survives being wrong at every status: one act, at the table, doable today, and it teaches something even if the read is off. The sentence that would serve me more than the reader is any line that makes 'the pull of what might be felt' sound lovely — if it flatters the condition instead of showing its cost, it goes.
